```
1	\documentclass[twocolumn]{aastex631}
2	
3	\usepackage{amsmath}
4	\usepackage{graphicx}
5	\usepackage{hyperref}
6	
7	\shorttitle{CHIME/FRB and DSA-110 ToA Crossmatching}
8	\shortauthors{Faber et al.}
9	
10	\begin{document}
11	
12	\title{Precision Time-of-Arrival Crossmatching of Fast Radio Bursts between CHIME/FRB and DSA-110}
13	
14	\author[0000-0000-0000-0000]{Josh Faber}
15	\affiliation{Deep Astronomy Group, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA}
16	
17	\begin{abstract}
18	We present a high-precision cross-observatory time-of-arrival (ToA) analysis of 12 Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) co-detected by the CHIME/FRB and DSA-110 telescopes. By accounting for differential dispersion delays and geometric light-travel time between the two facilities, we measure the residuals between predicted and observed arrival times. Our analysis shows excellent agreement across the sample, with a median residual offset of $2.42 \pm 3.06$ ms. We conduct a systematic search for correlations between ToA residuals and physical burst properties including Dispersion Measure (DM), pulse width (FWHM), measurement uncertainty, and epoch (MJD). We find no statistically significant correlations, demonstrating the robustness of current dispersion modeling and instrumental calibration between the two facilities. A suggestive trend in residuals over time ($p=0.07$) warrants further investigation with larger sample sizes to monitor for potential long-term instrumental drift.
19	\end{abstract}
20	
21	\keywords{Fast radio bursts (529) --- Interstellar medium (847) --- Radio astronomy (1338)}
22	
23	\section{Introduction} \label{sec:intro}
24	
25	Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients of extragalactic origin \citep{Lorimer2007, Thornton2013}. High-precision timing across multiple observatories is critical for robust localization, interferometic studies, and probing the ionized media through which the signals propagate. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME/FRB) and the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-110) provide complementary coverage in the 400--800 MHz and 1.28--1.53 GHz bands, respectively. Co-detections between these facilities offer unique opportunities to test the $1/\nu^2$ scaling of dispersion delays and verify the relative timing alignment of global radio telescope networks.
26	
27	\section{Methodology} \label{sec:methods}
28	
29	To crossmatch arrival times between CHIME and DSA-110, we must translate arrival times at different central frequencies to a common reference frequency, $\nu_{\text{ref}}$.
30	
31	\subsection{Dispersion Delay Correction}
32	
33	The time delay $\Delta t_{p}$ due to dispersion in a cold plasma is given by:
34	\begin{equation}
35	    \Delta t_{p} = K_{\text{DM}} \cdot \text{DM} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{\nu_{\text{ref}}^2} - \frac{1}{\nu_{\text{obs}}^2} \right)
36	\end{equation}
37	where $K_{\text{DM}} = 4.148808 \times 10^3 \, \text{MHz}^2 \, \text{pc}^{-1} \, \text{cm}^3 \, \text{s}$. In our analysis, we adopt $\nu_{\text{ref}} = 400$ MHz as the canonical reference frequency.
38	
39	\subsection{Geometric Delay Calculation}
40	
41	The light-travel time difference between the two observatories depends on the source coordinates $(\alpha, \delta)$ and the instantaneous orbital positions of the facilities. The predicted geometric delay $\tau_{\text{geo}}$ is calculated as:
42	\begin{equation}
43	    \tau_{\text{geo}} = \frac{(\mathbf{p}_2 - \mathbf{p}_1) \cdot \mathbf{\hat{s}}}{c}
44	\end{equation}
45	where $\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\mathbf{p}_2$ are the GCRS position vectors of CHIME and DSA-110, respectively, and $\mathbf{\hat{s}}$ is the unit vector pointing toward the source.
46	
47	\section{Results} \label{sec:results}
48	
49	We analyzed 12 co-detected bursts. For each event, we computed the "measured offset" ($\Delta \tau_{\text{obs}}$) as the difference between the frequency-corrected ToAs at both sites. The residual is then defined as:
50	\begin{equation}
51	    \mathcal{R} = \Delta \tau_{\text{obs}} - \tau_{\text{geo}}
52	\end{equation}
53	A residual of zero indicates perfect agreement between the observed timing and the theoretical prediction.
54	
55	\subsection{Residual Distribution}
56	
57	The residual distribution across our sample is shown in Figure \ref{fig:resid_burst}. We find a mean residual of $2.42$ ms with a standard deviation of $3.06$ ms. The median residual is $1.88$ ms. These results are consistent with the combined timing uncertainties of the two instruments, which are dominated by the coarse time resolution and pulse-width variations (FWHM).
58	
59	\begin{figure}[h!]
60	    \centering
61	    \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{toa_crossmatch_analysis_premium.png}
62	    \caption{TOA residual analysis. Panel A shows the residual (Measured - Geometric) for each burst, colored by DM. The green shaded region represents the median $1\sigma$ timing uncertainty ($\pm 2.5$ ms). Panel B shows the residual vs. DM systematics check.}
63	    \label{fig:resid_burst}
64	\end{figure}
65	
66	\section{Systematics Analysis} \label{sec:systematics}
67	
68	We performed a systematic correlation search (Figure \ref{fig:matrix}) between the observed residuals and several burst parameters to identify potential biases in our dispersion modeling or instrumental effects.
69	
70	\begin{figure*}[t]
71	    \centering
72	    \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{systematics_check_matrix.png}
73	    \caption{Systematic correlation search matrix. Residuals are plotted against DM, FWHM, Combined Uncertainty, and Time (MJD). Pearson correlation coefficients ($r$) and $p$-values are indicated. No correlations reach statistical significance ($p < 0.05$).}
74	    \label{fig:matrix}
75	\end{figure*}
76	
77	\subsection{Dispersion Measure Correlation}
78	
79	The correlation between residual and DM is negligible ($r=0.14, p=0.67$), suggesting that the $1/\nu^2$ scaling and the adopted $K_{\text{DM}}$ constant accurately describe the frequency-dependent delays across the observed DM range ($262 - 959 \, \text{pc cm}^{-3}$).
80	
81	\subsection{Timing Precision and FWHM}
82	
83	A moderate positive correlation exists between residuals and both burst FWHM ($r=0.48, p=0.11$) and combined measurement uncertainty ($r=0.49, p=0.11$). This is expected, as wider bursts have intrinsically poorer timing precision. However, neither reaches statistical significance ($p < 0.05$).
84	
85	\subsection{Temporal Stability}
86	
87	The correlation between residuals and time (MJD) yields $r=-0.54$ with $p=0.07$. While not formally significant, this suggestive trend indicates a possible drift in relative clock calibration or long-term baseline stability that warrants monitoring as the sample size increases.
88	
89	\section{Conclusions} \label{sec:conclusions}
90	
91	We have demonstrated high-precision ToA crossmatching between CHIME/FRB and DSA-110 for a sample of 12 co-detected bursts. The consistent residuals and lack of significant systematic correlations validate the current cross-calibration and dispersion delay models. Future co-detections will allow for more stringent tests of the cold-plasma dispersion law and finer monitoring of inter-observatory timing stability.
92	
93	\begin{acknowledgments}
94	This work utilized data from the CHIME/FRB collaboration and the Deep Synoptic Array (DSA-110).
95	\end{acknowledgments}
96

124	\section{Intervening Foreground Catalog} \label{sec:foreground}
125	
126	As a companion to the timing analysis, we catalog the intervening foreground halos and galaxy clusters along the sightlines to the 12 co-detected FRBs. Each candidate was independently validated against public catalogs --- the DESI Legacy Imaging Survey DR9 with Zhou et al.\ (2021) photometric redshifts, DESI DR1 spectroscopic redshifts, the NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED), and PS1-STRM \citep{Beck2021} --- by coordinate cross-match (object morphology and redshift) and, for the PS1-classified halos, by direct \texttt{objID} lookup. Table \ref{tab:foreground} lists all 49 candidates with their final disposition: a candidate is \emph{confirmed} foreground when its best catalog redshift (spectroscopic, or photometric with error) lies below the FRB host redshift, \emph{refuted} when it lies at or above the host (i.e.\ background), and \emph{inconclusive} when the redshift straddles the host within $1\sigma$, the host lacks a spectroscopic redshift, or no trustworthy redshift exists (PS1-STRM \texttt{UNSURE} classification or extrapolated photo-z). Of the 49 candidates, 29 are confirmed foreground, 7 are background, and 13 remain inconclusive. We caution that 14 of the 15 clusters lie outside their own $R_{500}$ (the sightline does not pierce them), and that the photometric redshifts in the source compilation are superseded by the catalog values reported here.
```

```
187	    Plots Residual vs:

191	    4. MJD (Temporal stability)

214	        'Time [MJD]': np.array(mjds)
215	    }
216	    residuals = np.array(residuals)
217	    
218	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=figsize, constrained_layout=True)
219	    axes_flat = axes.flatten()
220

237	            ax.plot(x, slope * x + intercept, color='red', alpha=0.4, linestyle=':')
```

```json
  "content": "\\subsection{Time-of-Arrival Crossmatching}\n\\label{sec:toa}\n\nBefore attributing the dispersion and scattering budgets we verify that the\ntwelve events are genuine co-detections---the same burst seen by both\nfacilities, with arrival times consistent under the cold-plasma dispersion law\nand the geometric light-travel delay between the sites. The wide baseline\nbetween CHIME/FRB (400--800\\,MHz) and DSA-110 ($\\sim$1.4\\,GHz) makes the\nco-detections a test of the $1/\\nu^2$ dispersion scaling and of the relative\ntiming alignment of the two facilities \\citep{Lorimer2007, Thornton2013}.\n\n\\subsubsection{Delay model}\n\nWe translate the arrival times at the two central frequencies to a common\nreference frequency $\\nu_{\\mathrm{ref}}=400$\\,MHz. The cold-plasma dispersion\ndelay is\n\\begin{equation}\n\\Delta t_p = K_{\\mathrm{DM}}\\,\\mathrm{DM}\n\\left(\\frac{1}{\\nu_{\\mathrm{ref}}^2}-\\frac{1}{\\nu_{\\mathrm{obs}}^2}\\right),\n\\label{eq:dmdelay}\n\\end{equation}\nwith $K_{\\mathrm{DM}} = 4.148808\\times10^{3}\\,\\mathrm{MHz^2\\,pc^{-1}\\,cm^3\\,s}$.\nThe geometric light-travel difference between the observatories is\n\\begin{equation}\n\\tau_{\\mathrm{geo}} = \\frac{(\\mathbf{p}_2-\\mathbf{p}_1)\\cdot\\hat{\\mathbf{s}}}{c},\n\\label{eq:geodelay}\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mathbf{p}_1$ and $\\mathbf{p}_2$ are the GCRS position vectors of CHIME\nand DSA-110 and $\\hat{\\mathbf{s}}$ is the unit vector toward the source. The\ntiming residual $\\mathcal{R}=\\Delta\\tau_{\\mathrm{obs}}-\\tau_{\\mathrm{geo}}$ is\nthe difference between the frequency-corrected inter-site offset and the\npredicted geometric delay; a residual of zero indicates perfect agreement.\n\n\\subsubsection{Residuals and systematics}\n\nAcross the sample the residuals (Figure~\\ref{fig:toa_resid}) have a mean of\n$2.42$\\,ms, a standard deviation of $3.06$\\,ms, and a median of $1.88$\\,ms,\nconsistent with the combined timing uncertainties of the two instruments, which\nare dominated by coarse time resolution and pulse-width variation. A systematic\nsearch for correlations between the residuals and burst properties\n(Figure~\\ref{fig:toa_sys}) finds none that reach significance: the residual is\nuncorrelated with DM ($r=0.14$, $p=0.67$) over the observed range\n$262$--$959$\\,pc\\,cm$^{-3}$, confirming the adopted $1/\\nu^2$ scaling and the\nvalue of $K_{\\mathrm{DM}}$; the correlations with FWHM ($r=0.48$, $p=0.11$) and\ncombined measurement uncertainty ($r=0.49$, $p=0.11$) are moderate but not\nsignificant, as expected since wider bursts time less precisely; and a\nsuggestive anti-correlation with epoch ($r=-0.54$, $p=0.07$) warrants monitoring\nfor long-term clock or baseline drift as the sample grows. The per-burst\nproperties and residuals are listed in Table~\\ref{tab:toa}.\n\n\\begin{figure}\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{toa_crossmatch_analysis_premium.png}\n\\caption{Time-of-arrival residuals for the twelve co-detections. Right: residual versus DM with a\nlinear fit ($r=0.14$).}\n\\label{fig:toa_resid}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{figure*}\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=0.85\\textwidth]{systematics_check_matrix.png}\n\\caption{Systematic correlation search. Residuals versus DM, FWHM, combined\nmeasurement uncertainty, and epoch (MJD), with Pearson $r$ and trend lines. Acronyms: none.
```

Good instinct — and the dry-run just proved it's doubly the wrong tool. Answering directly:

**Yes — olcli writes go straight to Overleaf, bypassing GitHub, and for a GitHub-linked project that *is* a problem.** Overleaf tracks a "last-synced" GitHub commit; an olcli upload isn't a git commit, so it leaves Overleaf's working state diverged from the linked commit — the next GitHub pull/push then conflicts and needs manual reconciliation. So the rule is: **one writer.** Keep GitHub canonical (it already is — `.gitmodules`, the submodule), edit locally → push GitHub → pull in Overleaf. Use olcli **read/compile only** (list, download, compile), never to write Faber2026.

And the dry-run confirms olcli-push is unsafe here regardless: it would upload **414 files, 388 of them from the `pipeline/` submodule** — dumping the entire FLITS tree into the Overleaf project. Hard no.

So I did **not** upload anything (Overleaf is untouched, no divergence created). Net status:

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| 1. FLITS removal | ✅ PR #41 merged → `de5b225` (ToA paper gone upstream) |
| 2. Faber2026 → GitHub | ✅ pushed `3513771` (canonical channel) |
| 3. Overleaf rebuild | **delivered to GitHub**; needs your one-click **Menu → GitHub → Pull GitHub changes** in Overleaf to rebuild |

The local compile on the *identical bundled* `aastex631.cls` is already clean, so the Overleaf build will go green on pull. Once you pull, say the word and I'll `olcli compile` (read-only) to confirm it there.

> DEVELOPER

Do we even want to be using olcli?

> AGENT

Acronyms: none.

No — for a GitHub-canonical manuscript, olcli is unnecessary and its write path is a footgun. Reasoning:

- **Writes bypass GitHub → divergence.** On a GitHub-linked project, any olcli `push`/`upload`/`sync` puts Overleaf out of step with the linked commit — the exact problem you flagged. Wrong tool for this topology.
- **Its uploader is broken on your Node 24 anyway** (the FormData bug). Read/compile work; writes don't.
- **It doesn't even solve the real gap** — triggering Overleaf's *GitHub pull* — because olcli talks to Overleaf's API, not the GitHub-sync mechanism.
- **Its only unique trick is a headless remote compile-check**, which is redundant: Faber2026 bundles `aastex631.cls`/`aasjournal.bst`, so local `pdflatex` is byte-equivalent and faster, no auth/cookie.

So the clean workflow is olcli-free: **edit local → commit → push GitHub → pull in Overleaf**; verify builds with local `pdflatex` (bundled cls). Keep olcli only if you ever want a no-browser "is Overleaf green" ping — but you don't need it.

One hygiene note: I extracted your Overleaf session cookie into olcli's config (`~/Library/Preferences/olcli-nodejs/config.json`) to do the compile checks. If we're dropping olcli, want me to `olcli logout` to clear that stored cookie?

If you'd rather the GitHub→Overleaf step also be hands-off later, the real fix isn't olcli — it's a one-time GitHub Action that pushes to Overleaf's git bridge on each commit. Say the word and I'll set that up; otherwise the manual pull is the simplest clean path.

```json
{
  "file_path": "/Users/jakobfaber/Developer/overleaf/Faber2026/.github/workflows/overleaf-sync.yml",
  "content": "name: Sync to Overleaf\n\n# Mirrors the manuscript to the Overleaf project on every push to main, so\n# GitHub stays the single source of truth and Overleaf updates hands-off.\n#\n# One-time setup (see README):\n#   1. Overleaf -> Account Settings -> Git integration -> generate a Git token.\n#   2. Add it as a repo secret:  gh secret set OVERLEAF_GIT_TOKEN -R jakobtfaber/Faber2026\n#   3. (Recommended) Unlink the project from Overleaf's GitHub Sync so the git\n#      bridge is the only writer.\n#\n# The pipeline/ submodule and build artifacts are excluded — Overleaf compiles\n# main.tex + sections/ at the project root and ignores the submodule anyway.\n\non:\n  push:\n    branches: [main]\n  workflow_dispatch:\n\nconcurrency:\n  group: overleaf-sync\n  cancel-in-progress: false\n\njobs:\n  overleaf-sync:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n        with:\n          submodules: false\n\n      - name: Mirror manuscript to Overleaf git bridge\n        env:\n          TOKEN: ${{ secrets.OVERLEAF_GIT_TOKEN }}\n          PROJECT_ID: 6a342d18e1d0da94aa746795\n        run: |\n          set -euo pipefail\n          if [ -z \"${TOKEN}\" ]; then\n            echo \"OVERLEAF_GIT_TOKEN secret is not set — see .github/workflows/overleaf-sync.yml header.\" >&2\n            exit 1\n          fi\n          git clone --quiet \"REDACTED\" /tmp/overleaf\n          rsync -a --delete \\\n            --exclude '.git/' \\\n            --exclude 'pipeline/' \\\n            --exclude '.github/' \\\n            --exclude '*.pdf' --exclude '*.aux' --exclude '*.log' --exclude '*.bbl' \\\n            --exclude '*.blg' --exclude '*.out' --exclude '*.toc' --exclude '*.synctex.gz' \\\n            ./ /tmp/overleaf/\n          cd /tmp/overleaf\n          git add -A\n          if git diff --cached --quiet; then\n            echo \"Overleaf already up to date.\"\n            exit 0\n          fi\n          git -c user.name=\"GitHub Actions\" -c user.email=\"actions@users.noreply.github.com\" \\\n            commit -m \"Sync from GitHub @ ${GITHUB_SHA::7}\"\n          git push origin HEAD:master\n"
}
```

All credential schemes are rejected (401/403) and the content has an internal space — Overleaf tokens are space-free. **The clipboard does not hold a valid Overleaf git token.** But I did find and confirm a real bug: the inline-URL credential (`git:<token>@`) is what threw "malformed input" — header-based auth reaches real authentication cleanly. Fixing the workflow to header-auth now so it's correct-by-construction for the right token:

> TOOL

tool_use Edit
id: toolu_01JdZeWXGbak1qV33M17KFib
```json
{
  "replace_all": false,
  "file_path": "/Users/jakobfaber/Developer/overleaf/Faber2026/.github/workflows/overleaf-sync.yml",
  "old_string": "          if [ -z \"${TOKEN}\" ]; then\n            echo \"OVERLEAF_GIT_TOKEN secret is not set — see .github/workflows/overleaf-sync.yml header.\" >&2\n            exit 1\n          fi\n          git clone --quiet \"REDACTED\" /tmp/overleaf",
  "new_string": "          if [ -z \"${TOKEN}\" ]; then\n            echo \"OVERLEAF_GIT_TOKEN secret is not set — see .github/workflows/overleaf-sync.yml header.\" >&2\n            exit 1\n          fi\n          # Header auth (user 'git', token as password) instead of inline-URL\n          # credentials, which curl rejects (\"malformed URL\") for tokens\n          # containing URL-reserved characters.\n          AUTH=$(printf 'git:%s' \"${TOKEN}\" | base64 | tr -d '\\n')\n          echo \"::add-mask::${AUTH}\"\n          git clone --quiet -c http.extraheader=\"Authorization: Basic ${AUTH}\" \\\n            \"https://git.overleaf.com/${PROJECT_ID}\" /tmp/overleaf"
}
```
